newsitem.title: USA: Bomb victims' families, survivors want McVeigh's death.
newsitem.headline: Bomb victims' families, survivors want McVeigh's death.

text.p: Many of those most touched by the Oklahoma City bombing clamoured for the death penalty for Timothy McVeigh on Tuesday and some asked for even harsher punishments as a jury prepared to decide his sentence.

Arlene Blanchard, a survivor of the 1995 bombing that killed 168 people, said death by lethal injection was "too good" for McVeigh and he should either be put in solitary confinement for life or simply be hung from a tree. "I know it sounds uncivilized but I want him to experience just a little of the pain and torture that he has put us through," she said.

A federal jury in Denver on Monday found McVeigh guilty of setting off the truck bomb that destroyed the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people, and the same jury will decide his punishment beginning on Wednesday.
There was little sentiment for mercy among bomb survivors, victims' relatives and others closest to the bombing.

"I don't think conventional methods should be used," said William Baay, a rescue worker who helped remove bodies from the rubble of the building. "They should amputate his legs with no anaesthesia ... and then set him over a bunch of bamboo shoots and let them grow up into him until he's dead."
Oklahoma religious leaders have expressed concern over the spirit of vengeance gripping some families.

"We do not want to be caught up in a lynch mob mentality, we do not want to be vindictive or engage in vengeance," the Rev. Louis Lamb told his Catholic congregation at St. Joseph's Old Cathedral on Sunday.

At the First United Methodist Church, associate pastor Todd Scoggins had a similar message: "I pray justice will be served ... but I pray even stronger that those who are bound by the chains of hatred will be set free."

Nevertheless, many residents said the Biblical notion of "an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth" backed up their demands for death and that the horror of McVeigh's crime means he stands in a category of his own.

"If an animal kills a human being they are summarily put to death and that's what this man needs. He needs to die because he is no longer human. He does not qualify to be called a human being any more," said Kathleen Treanor, whose 4-year-old daughter, Ashley Eckles, was killed in the blast.
Treanor plans to be a witness for prosecutors in the punishment phase of the trial.

The clamour for McVeigh's death reflected a growing trend in many states, where victims rights groups have gained significant power and voters are showing frustration with the lengthy legal delays in carrying out death sentences. A USA Today/CNN/Gallup poll after Monday's verdict showed 61 percent of respondents saying McVeigh should get the death penalty and only 31 percent saying he should get life in prison.
The federal government has not executed a prisoner in more than 30 years while Oklahoma has put nine to death since 1990.

The state most active in executions is neighbouring Texas, which has set a furious pace in recent months, drawing comparisons with Iran, Iraq and Saudi Arabia from the Amnesty International human rights group. Texas has executed 17 prisoners so far this year and plans to put another 10 more to death this month, including one on Tuesday night.

Oklahoma officials say they plan to file state murder charges against McVeigh for the 160 victims not named in the federal indictment and will push for the death penalty in case the federal punishment is too weak, is overturned on appeal or is never carried out.
Not everyone who lost family members in the bombing is pushing for McVeigh's death. Bud Welch's daughter, Julie, was killed but he said enough blood had been spilled without killing McVeigh as well.

"Death is the type of vengeance that I don't need and it serves no purpose for me. It has no redeeming value," Welch said, adding that keeping McVeigh alive and locked up could lead to him giving more details of the bombing plot.

"A dead man doesn't speak and I think McVeigh might tell us more. I would like to know more details about who all was really involved because I'm not at all convinced these (McVeigh and alleged co-conspirator Terry Nichols) are the only two people involved," he said.
